871.event_title: The Pig War on San Juan Island
871.place: San Juan Island, Washington Territory, United States
871.event: On 15 June 1859 the American settler Lyman Cutlar shot a pig belonging to the British Hudson's Bay Company that was rooting in his garden on San Juan Island, whose ownership both Britain and the United States claimed. When British authorities threatened to arrest him, American troops under Captain George Pickett landed, British warships arrived, and by the end of August hundreds of soldiers and dozens of guns faced each other. General Winfield Scott and Governor James Douglas agreed a joint military occupation, and the dispute was settled peacefully by arbitration in 1872, with the pig as the only casualty.
871.explanation: A petty quarrel over a garden and a pig came close to dragging two great powers into war, showing how easily trifling hostility can grow beyond anyone's control.
871.tie_back: The kural warns that enmity has no good in it and should not be courted even in jest, and the Pig War shows how a trivial grievance nearly became a real war.
871._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of how trivial hostility can escalate, though the event is about a minor quarrel rather than enmity sought for sport.

872.event: In March 1762 the Parlement of Toulouse condemned and executed the Huguenot merchant Jean Calas, convicted of murdering his son to stop him converting to Catholicism. Voltaire took up the case and, through a vigorous campaign of letters and pamphlets, including his Treatise on Tolerance of 1763, convinced much of European opinion that the judges had been swayed by anti-Protestant prejudice. A 50-judge royal panel reversed the conviction on 9 March 1765 and the government paid the family an indemnity.
872.explanation: One writer armed only with a pen discredited a powerful court before all of Europe and helped launch the movement for religious toleration and legal reform in France.
872.tie_back: The Toulouse judges learned that the hostility of a man whose plough is the word reaches further and lasts longer than that of any warrior.
872._accuracy_note: A very close fit for the danger of making enemies of those who wield words, though the judges did not knowingly choose Voltaire as their enemy.

873.place: Paraguay and the Rio de la Plata region, South America
873.event: Under Francisco Solano Lopez, Paraguay became entangled in disputes with Brazil and Argentina and in Uruguay's civil war, seized Brazilian vessels, attacked Brazilian territory and declared war on Argentina. Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay then formed an alliance against Paraguay in 1865, and the small country fought all three for five years. By the war's end in 1870 Paraguay lay in ruins, having lost more than half of its population and large areas of territory.
873.explanation: A small state without allies that turned three neighbours against it at once suffered one of the most devastating defeats in modern history.
873.tie_back: The kural calls the one who stands alone yet makes enemies of many more senseless than a madman, and Paraguay's war against three neighbours shows the cost of that choice.
873._accuracy_note: A strong fit for a lone power incurring many enemies; historians debate how far Lopez alone provoked the war, so the event field sticks to documented actions.

874.event_title: De Gaulle and Adenauer sign the Elysee Treaty
874.event: On 22 January 1963 French President Charles de Gaulle and West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer signed a treaty of friendship between their two countries, long-standing enemies. The treaty set up regular consultations at every level of government on foreign, defence and youth policy and led to the Franco-German Youth Office. The two leaders had begun their rapprochement at Colombey-les-Deux-Eglises in 1958 and marked it publicly at a reconciliation mass in Reims Cathedral.
874.explanation: Two long-standing enemies became the closest of partners, and their friendship became a foundation of European integration and peace.
874.tie_back: The kural says the world rests on the greatness of those who turn enemies into friends, and the Elysee Treaty turned Europe's oldest rivalry into a lasting friendship.
874._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of turning enmity into friendship, with wide benefits beyond the two nations.

875.event: Facing a Cold War rivalry with the Soviet Union and two decades of hostility with the People's Republic of China, the Nixon administration opened a secret channel to Beijing through Pakistan. Nixon travelled to China from 21 to 28 February 1972, becoming the first US president to visit the mainland while in office, and the visit ended with the Shanghai Communique. The State Department's historians record that the administration saw the Sino-Soviet split as an opportunity to build a relationship with Beijing that would counterweigh Moscow, and a US-Soviet summit followed in May 1972.
875.explanation: By reaching out to one of its two great adversaries, the United States changed the balance of the Cold War and gained leverage with the other.
875.tie_back: The kural advises that one facing two enemies should make one of them an ally, which is exactly the strategy of the opening to China.
875._accuracy_note: A very close fit to the two-enemies strategy, though the United States was not alone and without allies as the kural's first condition supposes.

876.event_title: The first Non-Aligned summit meets in Belgrade
876.event: In September 1961 leaders of about two dozen countries met in Belgrade for the first conference of the Non-Aligned Movement, founded by Josip Broz Tito of Yugoslavia, Jawaharlal Nehru of India, Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt, Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana and Sukarno of Indonesia. At the height of the Cold War, the member states declined to join either the American-led or the Soviet-led bloc. The conference adopted a declaration against colonialism and an appeal for peace addressed to both superpowers.
876.explanation: Newly independent nations chose to keep a careful distance from both rival blocs, neither binding themselves to one nor making an open enemy of the other.
876.tie_back: The kural counsels that in a time of crisis one should neither commit to nor break with either side, which is the stance non-alignment took during the Cold War.
876._accuracy_note: A good illustration of guarded neutrality between powerful parties, though the kural speaks of one person's dealings in crisis rather than a policy of states.

877.event_title: The Ghost Army deceives the enemy in Europe
877.event: The US Army's 23rd Headquarters Special Troops, a secret unit of about 1,100 men later called the Ghost Army, used inflatable tanks and vehicles, recorded battle sounds played through huge speakers, and fake radio traffic to make the enemy believe that large forces stood where there were few or none. In its largest operation, Operation Viersen in March 1945, it inflated more than 600 dummy vehicles to simulate two divisions while the Ninth Army crossed the Rhine. Its work stayed classified for decades, and its veterans were later awarded the Congressional Gold Medal.
877.explanation: By hiding gaps in the line and never letting the enemy see where it was thin, the Allies kept their opponents from exploiting their real weak points.
877.tie_back: The kural says never to show weakness before enemies, and the Ghost Army made a whole craft of hiding where Allied lines were weak.
877._accuracy_note: Fits the kural's second line on concealing weakness from enemies well, but not its first line about not confiding troubles to the unaware.

878.event_title: Meiji Japan ends the unequal treaties
878.place: Tokyo, Japan, and London, United Kingdom
878.event: From the 1850s Western powers imposed treaties on Japan that gave their citizens extraterritorial legal privileges and fixed Japan's customs duties, and they refused revision until Japan's institutions matched Western models. The Meiji government built modern legal codes, a constitution, an army and a navy, and in 1894 Britain signed a treaty agreeing to end extraterritoriality, which was abolished in 1899. Japan regained full tariff autonomy in 1911.
878.explanation: Japan won equal treatment not by a single blow against the treaty powers but by patiently building its own strength until their claims of superiority could no longer be sustained.
878.tie_back: The kural says that knowing the right method, making oneself strong and guarding oneself will make the enemy's arrogance fade by itself, which is how Japan ended the unequal treaties.
878._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of strength through preparation dissolving foreign arrogance, though the powers were treaty partners rather than open enemies, and Japan also fought wars in this period.

879.event: On 7 March 1936 Hitler repudiated the Locarno agreements and ordered German troops into the Rhineland, which had been demilitarized under the post-war settlement. Britain and France condemned the move but did not intervene; after consulting the British, the French cabinet decided not to risk a confrontation. Germany then fortified the Rhine frontier, and the Imperial War Museum notes that the success encouraged Hitler to pursue an even more aggressive foreign policy.
879.explanation: Historians widely see the failure to act in 1936, while German forces were still weak, as a missed chance to stop a danger that later cost far more to remove.
879.tie_back: The kural warns to cut down the thorn tree while it is young, and the Rhineland crisis is the classic case of a threat left to harden.
879._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's image of a threat ignored while small; the event field keeps to documented facts rather than counterfactuals.

880.event_title: The Holy League defeats the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto
880.place: Gulf of Patras, near Lepanto (Nafpaktos), Greece
880.event: After the Ottomans attacked Venetian Cyprus, the pope brought Spain, Venice and other states together in a Holy League, whose fleet under Don John of Austria met the Ottoman fleet near Lepanto on 7 October 1571. In about four hours of fighting the allies captured 117 galleys and virtually destroyed the Ottoman force. Britannica notes that the battle destroyed the myth of Turkish naval invincibility, even though Venice later surrendered Cyprus in 1573.
880.explanation: Lepanto mattered less for the territory it won than for breaking the confidence of a power that had seemed unbeatable at sea.
880.tie_back: The kural says those who cannot break the pride of hostile foes hardly live, and Lepanto is remembered above all as the day that pride was broken.
880._accuracy_note: A good illustration of shattering an enemy's sense of invincibility, though the kural's claim that the passive are not truly alive is a rhetorical judgement no event can fully show.
